items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use Among Health Care Professionals in the United States and United Kingdom: Cross-National Survey.
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined AI use among 524 health care professionals in the United States and United Kingdom, focusing on current applications, access, barriers, and factors that could support adoption. AI use was common but varied across professional and national contexts, with findings highlighting the importance of evidence, organizational guidance, training, privacy safeguards, and integration into clinical workflows for responsible adoption.

items.title: Correction to: Abstract 4365705: Cardiology Medications and Medicare Spending: Opportunities for Savings Using Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company and Costco Member Prescription Program Pricing.
Radiation Vasculopathy of the Coronary Arteries: State-of-the Art Review.
items.abstract: Radiation-associated coronary artery disease (RACAD) is a distinct form of coronary artery disease with several specific biological and clinical aspects as well as key knowledge gaps. RACAD is prevalent in patients with cardiac exposure to radiotherapy. As radiotherapy is integral to the effective treatment of many thoracic malignancies, improved long-term survivorship is coupled with increased risk for RACAD. Ionizing radiation induces free radical generation and activation of proinflammatory cascades, leading to endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis. Risks for RACAD are determined both by radiotherapy, including the radiation dose and the proximity of coronary arteries to the radiotherapy field, and by patient-specific factors, such as younger age, higher baseline cardiovascular risk, and concurrent cardiotoxic systemic therapies. Importantly, radiotherapy delivery is highly individualized on the basis of tumor location and treatment strategy, resulting in heterogeneous coronary exposure to radiation and patient-to-patient variability. Clinical presentation may occur early, within 1 to 2 years, especially in patients with higher cardiac radiation doses (eg, lung or esophageal cancer), or after a latency period of 5 to 20 years with lower cardiac dose radiation exposure (eg, left-sided breast cancer). Patients generally present with symptoms similar to conventional coronary artery disease. However, RACAD symptoms may be underrecognized in cancer survivors due to overlapping treatment-related fatigue, pulmonary disease, or competing oncologic symptoms. Diagnosis and management generally follow standard coronary artery disease guidelines while incorporating cancer-specific considerations, such as planned oncologic surgeries, bleeding risk, postradiotherapy complications such as atretic internal mammary arteries, and cardiotoxic effects of systemic cancer therapies. Primary prevention of RACAD is critical, emphasizing advances in precision radiotherapy, including delivery techniques with improved coronary dosimetry, and cardiac shielding. Key knowledge gaps include understanding long-term outcomes with contemporary 3-dimensional conformal radiotherapy techniques, validated cancer-specific risk prediction models on the basis of coronary dosimetry, optimal surveillance protocols, targeted molecular pharmacotherapies, and risk analysis of percutaneous versus surgical management of RACAD. Prospective studies are needed to develop cancer- and dosimetry-specific risk calculators, validating cardioprotective interventions, and improving multidisciplinary cardio-oncology collaboration to optimize early detection of RACAD and timely intervention in the growing population of cancer survivors.

items.title: Mechanical Stress Induces Nuclear Envelope Rupture in Melanoma Cells to Reorganize Tumor-Stromal Interactions.
items.abstract: Growth-induced solid stress and fluid pressure contribute to tumor progression and drug resistance. Beyond tumor endogenous physical forces, cells in the tumor microenvironment may also experience external macroscopic mechanical stress, and some tumors preferentially develop in weight-bearing regions with higher focal pressure. Characterization of the impact of macroscopic mechanical stress on the tumor microenvironment could help uncover the mechanistic links between external mechanical forces and increased tumor incidence. Here, we showed that recurrent macroscopic mechanical stress disrupts nuclear envelope integrity, leading to spatial reorganization and fibroblast subtype changes at the tumor-stromal interface. In mouse models of plantar melanoma, exogenous mechanical stress induced nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells and increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblasts. Reduction of nuclear envelope integrity through inducible deletion of Lmna likewise increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblast generation. Co-culture with myofibroblasts promoted nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells in 3D culture, suggesting a positive feedback loop. In addition, mechanical stress-driven transcriptomic changes in tumor and stromal cells were observed alongside enhanced lymph node metastasis and immunotherapy resistance. Analysis of human melanoma samples revealed mechanical stress-associated stromal remodeling and a higher incidence of lymph node metastasis in tumors arising in mechanically stressed regions, although these features were not significantly associated with overall survival. Together, these findings suggest that macroscopic mechanical stress may influence cancer progression by inducing nuclear envelope damage and reshaping tumor-stromal interactions.

items.title: Gut Microbiota and Immunotherapy: Baseline 16S rRNA Profiling as a Pragmatic Tool for Clinical Stratification.
items.abstract: The gut microbiota is a complex and dynamic ecosystem involved in the modulation of host immune responses. Accumulating evidence links gut microbial composition to the efficacy and toxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), although most evidence supporting microbiota-based biomarkers remains observational. Higher baseline alpha-diversity has been associated with favorable outcomes in several cohorts, but these associations are not uniform, and individual taxonomic signatures show substantial inter-study variability. In this perspective, we discuss baseline microbiota profiling as a promising investigational approach to patient stratification in immuno-oncology. Despite its methodological limitations, 16S rRNA sequencing remains a scalable, reproducible, and clinically feasible approach compared with more complex techniques such as shotgun metagenomics. Standardization of sampling procedures, sequencing methodologies, and bioinformatic pipelines is essential for the reliable implementation of microbiota-based biomarkers in routine clinical care. Integrating gut microbiota assessment into pre-treatment evaluation may improve patient selection and support a more biologically informed approach to immunotherapy. The human gut contains trillions of bacteria and other microorganisms that play an important role in keeping the body healthy, including helping the immune system work properly. Recent research shows that these gut microbes can also influence how well cancer treatments called immunotherapies work. In particular, patients with a more diverse and balanced mix of gut bacteria before starting treatment tend to respond better and live longer, while those with an imbalanced gut microbiota may have poorer outcomes. In this article, we suggest that analyzing gut bacteria before treatment could help doctors better understand which patients are more likely to benefit from immunotherapy. One commonly used method to study gut bacteria, called 16S rRNA sequencing, looks at the types and variety of bacteria present. Although more advanced techniques exist, this method is relatively simple, cost-effective, and suitable for use in clinical settings. However, to make this approach reliable in everyday medical practice, it is important to standardize how samples are collected, analyzed, and interpreted. By including gut microbiota analysis as part of routine checks before starting immunotherapy, doctors may be able to make more informed decisions and personalize treatment strategies, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

items.title: Professional Stakeholders' Perspectives on Early Screening for Type 1 Diabetes in Children: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Early screening for type 1 diabetes (T1D) is receiving increasing attention as presymptomatic screening initiatives and disease-modifying therapies continue to expand. However, the perspectives of professional stakeholders, who play a pivotal role in implementation, patient engagement, and health system preparedness, have not been systematically synthesised. We conducted a systematic review to examine professional views on paediatric early T1D screening. Following PRISMA guidelines, six databases (Medline, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ASSIA) and grey literature were searched through January 2026. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly involving paediatricians and diabetes specialists; nurses, genetic counsellors, policymakers, and other healthcare professionals were represented in few studies. Methodological appraisal using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) identified recurring limitations in sample representativeness and potential nonresponse bias. Given the heterogeneity and primarily descriptive nature of the study design and outcomes, findings were synthesised narratively. Professional perspectives varied according to the population targeted, professional group studied, screening scenario, and the implementation context. Where directly compared, support was greater for at-risk than for general-population screening. Reported benefits included diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) prevention, earlier clinical engagement, and improved preparedness for families. However, concerns persisted regarding psychosocial burden, workforce capacity, and unclear referral and follow-up pathways. More favourable evaluations were reported in some structured programmes, although these findings may reflect reliance on existing infrastructures and targeted participant selection. By consolidating previously fragmented evidence, this review identifies recurring clinical, psychosocial, and organisational considerations relevant to paediatric T1D screening. These findings primarily reflect clinical perspectives and indicate conditional rather than uniform support. Further studies should evaluate how standardised pathways, professional training, and integrated psychosocial support affect the feasibility and acceptability of screening across different healthcare contexts.

items.title: Sequential transarterial radioembolization and atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.abstract: Yttrium-90 transarterial radioembolization (TARE) combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors has been investigated as a potential therapeutic strategy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, evidence supporting its addition to current standard systemic therapy remains limited. We aimed to compare clinical outcomes in patients with advanced HCC treated with TARE followed by atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (TARE-Atezo/Bev) and Atezo/Bev alone. This retrospective cohort study included systemic therapy-naïve patients with advanced HCC treated with Atezo/Bev alone or TARE-Atezo/Bev at a single tertiary hospital between 2018 and 2025. Baseline characteristics were adjusted using propensity score matching (PSM) and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and the secondary outcome was progression-free survival (PFS). A total of 156 eligible patients were enrolled, including 93 in the Atezo/Bev group and 63 in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group. In the unmatched cohort, median OS was significantly longer in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group than in the Atezo/Bev group (14.1 vs 6.4 months; hazard ratio=0.43, 95% confidence interval = 0.29-0.63; p < 0.001), with consistent results after PSM (p = 0.01) and IPTW (p < 0.001). Although PFS was comparable between groups in the overall cohort, patients with Child-Pugh class A (OS: 14.6 vs 7.1 months; PFS: 7.7 vs 6.3 months) or ALBI grade 1 (OS: 21.4 vs 8.3 months; PFS: 8.1 vs 5.7 months) had significantly longer OS and PFS in the TARE-Atezo/Bev group, with similar results after adjustment. Sequential TARE-Atezo/Bev may improve survival compared with Atezo/Bev alone in patients with advanced HCC and well-preserved liver function. QuestionThe survival benefit of yttrium-90 TARE followed by Atezo/Bev compared with Atezo/Bev alone remains uncertain given limited evidence in advanced HCC. FindingsTARE followed by Atezo/Bev was associated with significantly longer OS than Atezo/Bev alone, with both OS and PFS improved in patients with advanced HCC and preserved liver function. Clinical relevanceSequential TARE followed by Atezo/Bev may offer a survival advantage in selected patients with advanced HCC, supporting the integration of locoregional and systemic therapies.

items.title: HVSnp: A manually curated database of human SNPS associated with viral infections.
items.abstract: We developed the "HVSnp: Human Viruses SNP-related database, a curated database". HVSnp is exclusive to the human SNPs studied and related to viral diseases, with manually mined and curated information from public SNP databases and scientific articles. We used MySQL (version 8.0) due to the easy management and the Looker Studio online availability. Among the output information, we have SNP identification, reference, alternative, and risk alleles, chromosome, gene, and gene function, summary, among others. In total, HVSnp contains eighteen viral diseases and 2020 records: Adenovirus (17 SNPs), Chikungunya (7), COVID-19 (314), Cytomegalovirus (54), Dengue (62), Epstein-Barr (54), Hepatitis A (3), Hepatitis B (380), Hepatitis C (166), Herpes (8), Human immunodeficiency virus (479), Papillomavirus (87), Influenza (74), Measles (68), Respiratory syncytial virus (50), Sars-CoV (80), West Nile (68), and Zika (49). As one SNP can be associated with more than one virus, the number of unique SNPs is 1691 and 651 genes. HVSnp has supplementary information obtained in articles for the summary elaboration, which contains the most significant results described in the literature about a possible relationship between SNPs and viruses. The database is available at URL: https://lookerstudio.google.com/s/pGUC7m538gQ.

items.title: Malignant Ascites Harbors Immune Niche with IL-10 Enriched Effector Dysfunction and Persistent Cancer-Binding IgG.
items.abstract: Malignant ascites provides a window into cancer-immune interactions in the peritoneal cavity. Using Cytometry by Time of Flight (CyTOF), we analyzed ascitic immune cells collected from patients with advanced gastrointestinal cancers, nonmalignant forms of hepatitis (NMH), and healthy control peripheral blood mononuclear cells (HC PBMCs). Compositionally, ascitic immune cells shared a myeloid-rich, B and naïve T cell-low signature relative to HC PBMCs. Underneath the shared ascitic compositional signature, three major functional immunophenotypes emerged in response to exogenous stimulation along a suppressive to cytotoxic axis, aligning with Luminex measurements of ascitic cytokine levels: IL-10 enriched, Nonpolarized, and Granzyme B (GZMB) enriched. In our cohort, the IL-10 enriched functional immunophenotype was exclusive to samples from patients with cancer while the GZMB enriched response was dominated by NMH samples. Ascites from patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) contained a persistent anti-cancer humoral response characterized by IgG that bound to autologous ascitic PDAC cells and multiple allogeneic PDAC cell lines.

items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of HCV Screening in Emergency Departments Using DETECT Hep C Trial Results.
items.abstract: Nontargeted hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening in emergency departments (EDs) has been demonstrated to identify more patients with HCV than targeted screening. Cost-effectiveness is key to strategy selection; however, the cost-effectiveness of these strategies in EDs remains unknown. To compare clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness of 2 novel ED-based HCV screening strategies with no ED HCV screening. In this economic evaluation study, a cohort of individuals presenting to the ED in the US was simulated with data from the Determining Effective Testing in Emergency Departments and Care Coordination on Treatment Outcomes for Hepatitis C Screening (DETECT Hep C) trial using the Hepatitis C Cost-Effectiveness (HEP-CE) model from a health sector perspective. Using data from EDs at Denver Health Medical Center, Johns Hopkins Hospital, and the University of Mississippi Medical Center, 3 strategies were simulated over a lifetime horizon, including (1) no ED HCV screening, (2) targeted HCV screening, and (3) nontargeted HCV screening. Data were collected from November 2019 to August 2022 and analyzed from December 2021 to July 2026. HCV screening in the ED. The primary outcomes were remaining life expectancy, quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), and costs (2024 US dollars). An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to future costs and benefits when calculating ICERs. An ICER of less than $100 000 per QALY gained was considered cost-effective. A simulated cohort with a total of 500 million individuals (mean [SD] age, 46.3 [17.2] years; 264.4 million male [52.88%]) were included in this analysis. Nontargeted HCV screening yielded the best clinical and cost-effectiveness outcomes in the base case cohort, with 65.89% of infections being cured, a discounted cost of $214 465, discounted quality-adjusted life expectancy of 15.8723 QALYs, and an ICER of $12 820 per QALY gained. Compared with nontargeted HCV screening, no ED HCV screening and targeted HCV screening, respectively, had fewer infections cured (65.60% and 65.88%), lower QALYs (15.8717 QALYs and 15.8721 QALYs), and similar discounted costs ($214 467 and $214 462). Absolute benefits appeared narrow because over 90% of those screened did not have HCV; however, benefits were clear among those living with HCV infection. Results of this economic evaluation study suggest that nontargeted HCV screening was cost-effective when compared with no HCV screening or targeted HCV screening in the ED. Implementing routine nontargeted HCV screening in emergency departments provides good economic value and could be an important pillar of HCV elimination.

items.title: Hepatocellular carcinoma screening in a tertiary hospital. What are we missing?
items.abstract: Screening for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) aims to detect early tumors, with a positive impact on survival. In clinical practice there are several challenges on the application of HCC screening: patients with unknown liver disease, poor patient adherence or problems in the health care system, leading to an underperformance. We aim to evaluate the performance of the HCC screening, the reasons of missed or delayed diagnosis, and prognostic implications in patients with HCC in a tertiary center. Retrospective study including patients with an HCC diagnosis, that have been discussed by a liver tumors board from 2020 to 2023 in a tertiary hospital. HCC screening was defined according to the EASL recommendations. Considering the target population for screening, subgroups were considered and compared: (a) diagnosed through screening; (b) missed screening due to suboptimal patient adherence and/or systemic healthcare inefficiencies; (c) undiagnosed advanced chronic liver disease (uACLD), that would have indication for surveillance if already diagnosed. For patients diagnosed through screening, we considered a margin of 2 months (8 months) as "complete surveillance" and between 8 to 12 months as "incomplete surveillance". To access the survival benefit, we compared the overall survival of the screened population and those do not diagnose through screening. We included 174 patients, 136 had advanced chronic liver disease (ACLD): 70% Child-Pugh (CP) A; 20% CP B; 10% CP C. The most common etiologic factor was excessive alcohol consumption (37%). The proportion of patients diagnosed in screening was 26%. Regarding Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage at diagnosis, 4% BCLC-0, 37% BCLC-A, 10% BCLC-B, 33% BCLC-C and 15% BCLC-D. Patients in subgroup (a) had HCC diagnosed at earlier stages (BCLC-0 and BCLC-A). The subgroup (c) had a higher proportion CP B and C (p = 0.008), vascular invasion (p = 0.01), extrahepatic involvement (p = 0.052) and hepatic dysfunction according to ALBI score (p < 0.001) at time of diagnosis. Overall survival was significantly higher for screened group. In our cohort, only about a quarter of HCC cases were diagnosed through screening, with impact on survival. Among patients with indication for screening, only one third achieved diagnostic yield. Our findings emphasize the need to improve HCC screening strategies and the pivotal role of primary care in the early diagnosis of underlying liver disease.

items.title: Integrating Non-Invasive Liver Assessment into Screening Colonoscopy: A Prospective Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Steatotic liver disease is underdiagnosed despite guideline recommendations for risk-based case-finding. Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening colonoscopy engages a prevention-oriented, healthcare-seeking population in whom liver disease may go undetected. We assessed the feasibility, acceptance, and yield of non-invasive liver assessment integrated into screening colonoscopy visits. This prospective cross-sectional study enrolled adults aged ≥50 years attending screening colonoscopy. Individuals with known chronic liver disease were excluded. Participants underwent hepatic ultrasound and point shear wave elastography. Liver stiffness measurements (LSM) were interpreted using prespecified thresholds of 1.30, 1.50, and 1.70 m/s (∼5, 7, and 9 kPa, respectively). We assessed whether risk-factor-based criteria would have identified participants with elevated stiffness, and evaluated the Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4) against LSM thresholds. Of 692 adults offered participation, 610 enrolled (88.2% acceptance); one was excluded for decompensated heart failure. Reliable LSM was obtained in 578 of 609 (94.9%). Ultrasound-defined steatosis was identified in 55.5%. LSM exceeded 1.30 m/s in 25.3%; 9.0% and 5.0% met thresholds consistent with significant fibrosis (≥1.50 m/s) and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (≥1.70 m/s), respectively. Among participants with LSM ≥1.50 m/s, exposure profiles were metabolic in 63.5%, mixed metabolic-alcohol in 21.2%, and alcohol-related in 15.4%. Risk-factor criteria were met by 76.6% and captured 46/52 participants with LSM ≥1.50 m/s. At this threshold, FIB-4 showed modest discrimination (AUROC 0.682); sensitivity decreased from 0.706 using a single threshold to 0.529 using age-adjusted thresholds. Opportunistic liver assessment integrated into screening colonoscopy was feasible, well accepted, and identified previously undetected steatosis and elevated LSM.

items.title: Increased risk of cancer in patients with mixed connective tissue disease: a population-based cohort study in Korea.
items.abstract: We conducted a nationwide, population-based cohort study to evaluate the risk of cancer in Korean patients with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) compared with the corresponding risk in the general population. Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service data, we identified 2,094 patients with newly diagnosed MCTD between 2004 and 2020 (16,409 person-years). Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) were calculated to compare the overall and site-specific cancer risks between patients with MCTD and the age- and sex-matched general population. The overall risk of cancer was significantly higher in patients with MCTD than in the general population (SIR 2.61, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.27-2.99). For site-specific cancers, both the risks of solid (SIR 2.46, 95% CI 2.12-2.84) and haematologic (SIR 6.81, 95% CI 4.36-10.13) cancers were elevated in patients with MCTD compared with the general population. Among solid cancers, increased risks were observed for several sites, including the lung, ovary, liver, pancreas, cervix, gallbladder/biliary tract, prostate, bladder, and oesophagus. Regarding haematologic cancers, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndrome, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma showed increased risks. The relative cancer risk was highest in patients aged 20-39 years (SIR 4.04, 95% CI 2.90-5.48) and during the first year after MCTD diagnosis (SIR 3.77, 95% CI 2.70-5.11). Patients with MCTD have an increased cancer risk, particularly haematologic cancer, compared with the general population. The cancer risk was particularly elevated in younger patients and during the first year after MCTD diagnosis. Key Points • Patients with MCTD have a higher overall risk of cancer, particularly haematologic cancer. • Cancer risk is particularly elevated during the first year after MCTD diagnosis, and clinicians should not overlook the possibility of cancer in younger patients with suggestive clinical features.

items.title: Body Roundness Index and Cancer Risk in Postmenopausal Women: Findings from the Women's Health Initiative.
items.abstract: Background Body Roundness Index (BRI) is an anthropometric measure that combines waist circumference and height. It reflects central adiposity more accurately than body mass index (BMI). Evidence linking BRI to long-term cancer risk, particularly in postmenopausal women, remains limited. Methods We examined associations between BRI and incident site-specific cancers (n=33,892) in 144,865 postmenopausal women aged 50-79 years at enrollment into the Women's Health Initiative and followed for a median of 17.9 years. BRI was assessed at baseline in all participants and at year 3 in 60% of participants. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations between BRI and cancer incidence, adjusting for sociodemographic, reproductive, and lifestyle factors. Results Higher BRI levels were associated with increased risks of kidney, endometrial, liver, esophageal, thyroid, colorectal, stomach, pancreas, bladder, breast, and lung cancers, and with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, particularly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Adjustment for BMI attenuated associations for endometrial, breast, and kidney cancers but strengthened those for liver, lung, and esophageal cancers. Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses and models incorporating repeated BRI measurements. Age-stratified (< /≥ 63 years) models indicated stronger associations for kidney cancer among younger women and a significant positive association for melanoma among older women. Conclusions Among postmenopausal women, higher BRI was associated with increased risk of cancer at multiple sites independently of BMI. These findings support an important role for central adiposity in cancer risk beyond overall body size. Impact In postmenopausal women, BRI may improve estimation of site-specific cancer risk beyond BMI by capturing central adiposity.

items.title: A Novel cccDNA-Binding Protein HSPA1B Promotes HBV Transcription and HBx-Mediated HCC Metastasis via Downregulating SOX4.
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) occurrence and progression are closely associated with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Heat shock protein family A member 1B (HSPA1B), a key member of the heat shock protein 70 family, has attracted extensive attention in viral infection research, yet its specific function in HBV-related HCC pathogenesis remains largely unknown. HSPA1B was identified as a cccDNA-binding protein using the biotin-avidin system, and its role in HBV infection and HCC progression was systematically investigated. In vivo experiments were performed using a mouse model established by tail vein injection of prcccDNA and pCMV-KRAB-Cre to evaluate the impact of HSPA1B on HBV transcription and replication. RNA sequencing was applied to HBV-infected HepG2-NTCP cells to analyze the differentially expressed genes regulated by HSPA1B, aiming to clarify the molecular mechanism underlying HSPA1B-mediated promotion of HBV transcription and replication. Meanwhile, Western blot, RT-qPCR, co-immunoprecipitation and Transwell assays were used to explore the relationship between HSPA1B and HBV-related HCC. We found that HSPA1B promoted HBV transcription and replication. Mechanistically, the increased expression of HSPA1B promoted HBV transcription and replication by downregulating SOX4 and enhancing the stability of the HBx protein. Further research indicated that HSPA1B can enhance the metastasis and invasion of HBx-mediated HCC. Collectively, these results demonstrate a novel function of HSPA1B in regulating HBV transcription and HBV-related HCC metastasis, indicating that HSPA1B may serve as a promising therapeutic target for HBV-associated HCC.
